### Query: "Fruitvale Transit Hub Phase II — Visioning initiative vote"

The three design scenarios — ranging from a market-driven approach to a maximum community benefit model — all meet those non-negotiable requirements. Community members will recommend a scenario to the council, which retains final authority. **Why the Comparison to Phase I Matters** Turner was a teenager when Phase I of the Fruitvale BART hub was completed. He watched the promises about local hiring and a community stabilization fund arrive in print and then dissolve in practice. The stabilization fund was underfunded. The local hiring outcomes were never publicly accounted for. The affordability units built in the first phase had no long-term lock. He is not alone in that memory. Rose Delgado, who represents District 3 and attended both community visioning sessions, told colleagues before the vote that Phase I left the neighborhood with infrastructure lessons it intended not to repeat. "This neighborhood has been patient," Delgado said from the dais. "Phase I was promised. Phase II needs to deliver."

The deadline has passed. The questions have not.

------------------------------------------------------------ FRUITVALE VOTED. NOW THE LAWYERS WRITE. By Carmen Delaine, City Hall Correspondent Eighty-nine residents showed up to the Fruitvale Transit Hub Phase II community visioning sessions. Eighty-two percent lived in Fruitvale. Sixty-six percent were Spanish-speaking. They ranked their preferences using a ranked-choice ballot. The results came back unambiguous: 52 percent first choice for the Community Benefit Maximum scenario. Eighty-seven percent ranked it in their top two. Mayor Santana issued a directive in response. "Fruitvale voted," Santana said. "Eighty-seven percent want the strongest community benefits. We honor that mandate." The directive to planning staff is specific: advance the Community Benefit Maximum scenario for City Council consideration in November. Binding commitments on small business rent locks for 30 years. Affordable housing at 35 percent with 100-year affordability protections via community land trust.

### Query: "Oakland Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline initiative vote"

### West Oakland Gets Safer as the Apprenticeship Bill It's Waiting On Heads to a Vote

By Luis Navarro | Bay Tribune Civic Affairs

---

West Oakland's violent crime numbers are at their lowest point in cycles. That is not a qualifier. That is not a "but." It is the first fact.

The second fact: the bill designed to build an economic life alongside that safety — the Oakland Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline — sat untouched at legislation-filed for four consecutive cycles before this one. Filed, announced, praised at a press conference. Then nothing.

Four cycles is a long time to wait on a promise.

---

Mayor Santana moved on it this cycle. She directed Councilmember Janae Rivers (D5) to bring INIT-007 to the council floor, and Rivers took it as the Oakland Progressive Party's own. That is a meaningful shift. A bill sitting in committee is a proposal. A bill on the floor is a reckoning.

---

# INIT-007 Apprenticeship Legislation Filed; Bill Introduction Queues Next Cycle

By M. Corliss

The Oakland Apprenticeship Initiative — INIT-007 — moved from concept to legislation-filed this cycle. Council Member Janae Rivers (D5, OPP) carries the bill; introduction is queued for the next council session.

The piece is small in word count and large in placement. The Apprenticeship Initiative is the workforce-pipeline lever for Phase II Baylight: 25 percent of Phase II construction jobs are designated for apprentices under the RFP terms now public (see Business, this edition). INIT-007 is the structure that makes those slots fillable from West Oakland, East Oakland, and Fruitvale instead of imported. Without it, the mandate is a number on a contract page. With it, the number becomes a pathway.

Rivers framed it tightly: "Oakland Oaks means Oakland youth in Oakland jobs. INIT-007 legislation-filed makes that the structural promise."
